title: Olivia Rodrigo Launches All-Women Daisy Chain Fields Festival to Benefit Charities
summary: Olivia Rodrigo is taking her advocacy to the main stage. On Monday, the Grammy-winning artist announced Daisy Chain Fields, her own all-women music festival set for August 29 in Irvine, California. The inaugural event boasts a powerhouse lineup: Chappell Roan, KATSEYE, Doechii, and Stevie Nicks are among the headliners, with Rodrigo herself also performing alongside acts like Bikini Kill, Garbage, Mitski, and the Breeders. Nicks is billed as one of three "special guests," joined by Karen O and Sarah McLachlan. "Truly never felt more excited to share a piece of news with you all," Rodrigo wrote on Instagram. "I've had a dream of doing this festival for years and I am so ecstatic it's finally coming true!!" The festival's mission is as bold as its lineup: 100 percent of net proceeds will go to charities dedicated to advancing and advocating for women and girls. Beneficiaries include Baby2Baby, Black Mamas Matter Alliance, Center for Reproductive Rights, and Planned Parenthood, among others. "I firmly believe that joy, community, and music can be the drivers of meaningful change," Rodrigo added. This isn't Rodrigo's first foray into philanthropy. In 2024, she launched her Fund 4 Good, raising over $2 million through her Guts World Tour for reproductive rights, education, and anti-domestic violence initiatives. Planned Parenthood honored her with its Catalyst of Change award in 2025. Daisy Chain Fields draws clear inspiration from Lilith Fair, the groundbreaking all-women festival founded by McLachlan in 1997—a connection underscored by McLachlan's appearance as a special guest. The announcement comes just 10 days after Rodrigo released her Billboard 200-topping third album, You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love. With Daisy Chain Fields, she's channeling her platform into a tangible force for good, proving that a concert can be more than just music—it can be a movement.
why_it_matters: Daisy Chain Fields shows how a teenage star can turn fame into a platform for concrete change, funneling millions toward women's health and safety. For middle-schoolers, it demonstrates that art, commerce, and activism don't have to be separate worlds—they can be stitched together to tackle issues that will directly affect their generation.

background_read: Lilith Fair, created by Sarah McLachlan in 1997, was a touring all-female music festival that raised over $10 million for women's charities before ending in 1999; it proved that women-led lineups could be commercially successful and socially impactful.

Olivia Rodrigo (a Grammy-winning singer-songwriter who rose to fame with hits like 'drivers license') has been outspoken about reproductive rights, especially after many U.S. states tightened abortion laws.

Planned Parenthood, one of the festival's beneficiaries, is a major nonprofit that provides reproductive healthcare, sex education, and advocacy; supporting it has become a rallying point for many young artists.
Benefit concerts are a long tradition: from George Harrison's Concert for Bangladesh in 1971 to modern events like FireAid, artists often use their fame to raise funds and awareness for crises.
All-women music festivals remain rare in an industry where headliners at major events are overwhelmingly male, making Daisy Chain Fields a notable statement about representation.

perspectives.description: Fans get to see a lineup stacked with female artists who rarely share a stage, celebrating women's creativity and solidarity. The money raised will directly fund organizations that help women and girls with healthcare, supplies, and legal support.

Skeptics point out that one-day festivals, while generous, often generate less long-term impact than sustained policy work. Some worry the focus on a single star's brand might overshadow the grassroots groups actually doing the daily work.

The festival consciously revives the model of Lilith Fair, which faced backlash in the 1990s for being 'too political' yet proved commercially viable. Daisy Chain Fields tests whether today's more fractured media landscape can still rally a broad audience around a feminist cause.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: Could this become a movement?
perspectives.description: If successful, Rodrigo's festival could inspire other major artists to launch similar benefit events, normalizing large-scale giving in the music industry. It also raises the question of whether the festival might expand to multiple cities or become an annual tradition.
